newsitem.title: ITALY: Defence lawyers urge clemency for ex-Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Defence lawyers urge clemency for ex-Nazis.

text.p: A lawyer for ex-Nazi Erich Priebke on Monday told a court trying him for his role in Italy's worst wartime massacre that he was obeying orders, like the American who dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima, and should be freed.
"Priebke obeyed an executive order," defence lawyer Giosue Naso said, referring to the 1944 massacre in which the 83-year-old former SS captain is charged with complicity.

"What could the American officer who was ordered to drop the Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki have done? Has he been tried for what he did? Obviously, history is always written by the winners," Naso said.
A lawyer for Priebke's co-defendant, SS major Karl Hass, 84, earlier told the court he should be set free because he had not participated in the planning of the massacre.

Priebke and Hass have each admitted shooting two victims of the 335 men and boys rounded up by the Germans and shot at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome as a reprisal for a bomb attack on Nazi troops. Seventy-five of the victims were Jews.
Priebke has in addition admitted ticking the names of victims of a list as they arrived at the caves.
"Hass...was only informed two hours before the start of the executions, so there could have been no premeditation," his lawyer Stefano Maccioni said.
A lawyer for the city of Rome told the court earlier this month the Germans deserved five life sentences each.

Military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano has demanded a life sentence for Priebke and 24 years for Hass, saying Priebke's crimes were aggravated by cruelty, brutality and premeditation while Hass could claim mitigating circumstances.
Priebke, who was extradited from Argentina in November 1995 where he had lived openly for nearly half a century, is being held under house arrest at a Roman Catholic monastery.

Hass appeared as a prosecution witness in Priebke's first trial, which ended in uproar last August when a military court ruled that Priebke was guilty of complicity in the massacre but could not be punished under a statute of limitations.
Protestors besieged the court and Priebke was re-arrested a few hours later. The verdict was quashed on appeal.
Hass reluctantly testified at the first trial from a hospital bed after injuring himself while trying to flee. He was arrested after admitting he too took part in the shootings.
